{{< generated ch04-hero >}}

Neural networks use the same features, losses and evaluation principles as the models you already know. This chapter makes their training machinery visible, then returns to the central scientific question: does the extra flexibility improve predictions on unseen examples?

## What you will be able to do

::: {.mm-outcomes-wrap}
- Trace shapes, dtypes and sample identities from a descriptor table to a prediction.
- Explain the difference between calculating gradients and updating parameters.
- Build a multilayer perceptron with an output and loss suited to its target.
- Train in mini-batches and use the correct training and evaluation modes.
- Restore an early-stopped checkpoint and assess dropout and weight decay.
- Compare a neural network with ridge regression using validation for selection and a final held-out test report.
:::

## Before you start

::: {.prereq}
Review NumPy shapes in [episode 1.2](../ch01-scientific-python/02-numpy-arrays.html), gradient descent in [episode 2.2](../ch02-ml-fundamentals/02-linear-regression.html), and the cross-validation and tuning workflow in [episodes 2.7–2.8](../ch02-ml-fundamentals/07-cross-validation.html). You should be able to distinguish training, validation and test data before adding a more flexible model.
:::

Use the course environment from [Chapter 0](../ch00-start-here/02-setup.html), which includes PyTorch. All examples and the lab run on a laptop CPU; the lab setup also supports Google Colab. The lessons use synthetic data or scikit-learn's bundled breast-cancer benchmark, and the lab reuses ESOL from Chapter 2.

## Check your understanding

Finish with the [ten-question checkpoint](checkpoint.html) and [chapter key points](key-points.html). If a model fails to learn, revisit the tensor, loss and loop contracts before changing its size. If it learns the training set but performs poorly on validation data, revisit the evaluation design and complexity controls.
